title: Build a wooden block marble run: set three drilled blocks so their holes meet, then roll the marble down into the cup
instruction: Build the marble run on the start beam: set the turn-down block on the beam over the beam's hole with its side hole facing left, set the turn-across block on the beam just left of it with its side hole against the first block's side hole, and set the straight block on top of the turn-across block. Then drop the blue marble into the straight block's top hole so it rolls down into the cup.
context: Wooden block marble runs are a staple of homes, nurseries and classrooms: drilled beech blocks are stacked loose so that a marble put in at the top finds its way to the bottom. Building one is stacking with a purpose. Each block has to be turned the right way round, because a turn block's side hole must face the block it feeds, and set down so its hole meets the next hole within a few millimetres; a block put down back to front or half a hole off leaves the marble stuck inside. The blocks are held only by their weight, so setting one down hard or brushing the stack moves the blocks already placed. The build is tested the way a child tests it: the marble goes in at the top and either drops out into the cup or it does not. Here the marble must fall, turn sideways into the next block, turn down again and drop through the start beam into a cup underneath.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. Blocks: a HABA Ball Track Large Basic Pack (HABA 1136, 42 solid beech pieces, 6 glass marbles, 40 mm base block; about 150 US dollars); its pieces are unpainted beech, about 0.7 g/cm3 (estimate). Every hole is 24 mm across (estimate from retailer photos against the 40 mm block; check with a ruler). 1) Start structure, already built: two plain 40 mm cubes stand on the table at (160, -38) and (160, 118); the drilled 160 x 40 x 40 beam (166 g) lies across them along y, centred at (160, 40), top 80 high; its one hole goes straight down through it at (160, 60), 100 from its near end. Under that hole stands the catch cup, a Winco SCP-15 1.5 oz stainless sauce cup (57 across the top, 38 across the base, 25 high; 22 g estimate), centred at (160, 60). 2) Three loose drilled 40 mm cubes stand in a row at x 250: the turn-down block at y 95 and the turn-across block at y 170 are two of the set's redirection blocks, each a cube with one bore that curves a quarter turn from the middle of one face to the middle of an adjacent face (35 g); the turn-down block stands with its holes in its bottom and in the side facing the robot, the turn-across block with its holes in its top and in the side facing away from the robot. The straight block at y 245 is a cube with one straight bore from its top face to its bottom face (32 g). 3) One 15 mm blue glass marble from the set (4.4 g, estimate) lies on the table at (150, 200), on a pencil cross. Goal layout (the README's picture): turn-down block on the beam over the beam's hole, side hole facing left; turn-across block on the beam beside it, 4 mm gap, side holes facing each other; straight block on the turn-across block. Frictions (estimates): beech 0.4, marble on beech 0.4. Both arms start at ready.
scoring: Judged at the end of the run from a photo, a ruler and the trial video. Three joints, each between two holes that meet: (1) beam to turn-down block: the turn-down block sits on the beam with its bottom hole over the beam's hole, the two hole centres within 6 mm of each other across the joint; (2) turn-down to turn-across block: their side holes face each other (within 20 degrees), the two hole centres within 6 mm of each other across the joint and the two faces at most 6 mm apart; (3) turn-across to straight block: the straight block sits on the turn-across block's top hole, centres within 6 mm across. A joint counts only with both blocks sitting flat (tilted at most 5 degrees, the upper block's face within 3 mm of the face below), still, and let go (no gripper within 3 cm), and with the start beam still lying on its two cubes. The marble run counts when, on the video, the marble went into the straight block's top hole after the gripper let go, stayed inside the blocks' holes and the drop below the beam, and lies in the cup (inside it, below the rim), moving under 2 cm/s, for 1 s. 1.0: all three joints and the marble run. 0.75: all three joints, marble not run into the cup. 0.5: two joints. 0.25: one joint. 0: no joint; doing nothing scores 0. A marble carried or dropped straight into the cup, or one that left the blocks on the way, earns nothing.
reset_notes: About one minute. Take the marble out of the cup and lay it on its pencil cross at (150, 200). Lift the straight, turn-across and turn-down blocks off and stand them back at x 250, y 245, 170 and 95: the turn-down block with its holes in its bottom and in the side facing the robot, the turn-across block with its holes in its top and in the side facing away. Check that the beam still lies on its two cubes with its hole straight over the cup (look down the hole) and put back anything that moved: cubes at (160, -38) and (160, 118), beam centred at (160, 40) with its hole at y 60, cup centred under the hole. If the marble rolled off the table, fetch it before the next trial. Return both arms to the ready pose.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at true size. Each drilled block is one free body made of convex pieces around an open 24 mm bore (estimate), 12-sided; the turn blocks' quarter-turn bore (centre-line radius 20 mm, estimate) is drawn as four straight 22.5-degree segments. Block, marble and cup masses, wood density and all frictions are estimates; rolling resistance is not modelled. The cup is modelled as 24 thin wall facets and a base.
